checks.prompt: A contact-centre platform needs live transcription of calls, spoken replies from a bot, translation for some callers, and a way to verify a caller's identity by voice — all under the organisation's existing cloud identity controls and data-residency rules. Which property of this platform is decisive, and what should temper the decision?
checks.explanation: The decisive property is breadth behind one integration: a single regional resource and one configuration object flow into recognition, synthesis, translation, speaker recognition and pronunciation assessment, with enterprise identity, network controls and regional data residency around them. The honest caveats are that it is cloud-only, that its expressive synthesis trails the specialist leader, and that a brand voice requires an application to a gated programme rather than cloning from a sample.
options: That one resource and one configuration object cover recognition, synthesis, translation, speaker recognition and pronunciation scoring behind a single toolkit, with the cloud's identity, network-control and data-residency plumbing around it — so four capabilities are one integration rather than four vendors. What should temper it is that everything is hosted, top-tier expressive synthesis is not its strongest suit, and a brand voice is available only through a gated programme rather than instant cloning
That it runs the models locally under your identity controls, so nothing leaves the network; the tempering factor is that it covers recognition only, so synthesis needs a second vendor
That it is the naturalness leader for synthesis; the tempering factor is that translation and speaker recognition are separate products with separate credentials
That it bills a single flat subscription across all features; the tempering factor is that language coverage is limited to a handful of locales

checks.prompt: Describe this platform as a switchboard with many lines. Name the three objects every task is built from and say what each decides. Explain what stays the same and what changes when you move from recognising speech to synthesising it. Then explain why the region is not merely a latency preference.
checks.expected: A correct answer must name the three objects and their roles. The configuration object carries WHO you are and the global settings: the credential — a key paired with its region, or an identity token — plus the recognition language, the synthesis voice and the output audio format. The audio configuration carries WHERE audio comes from or goes to: a microphone, a file, or a push or pull stream on input; a speaker, a file, or a stream on output; omitted, the system default is used. The worker object carries WHAT you are doing: a recogniser, a synthesiser, a translating recogniser, a speaker recogniser, a pronunciation assessor. What stays the same across tasks is the configuration object — the same credentials and resource flow into every feature — and what changes is the worker and the direction of the audio configuration. The region point must be made properly: the region is part of the endpoint and the resource is regional, so a key issued in one region simply does not authenticate against another — it is an identity-and-data-residency fact, not a choice of nearest datacentre, and getting it wrong produces an authentication failure rather than slower calls. A strong answer notes that failures generally do not raise: a call returns a result whose reason says it was cancelled, with details carrying the error code, so inspecting the reason rather than assuming success is part of using the toolkit correctly.

checks.prompt: A team transcribes hour-long support calls and finds each transcript contains only the caller's opening sentence. They also complain that their cheerful-sounding replies come out flat despite the markup specifying a cheerful style. What are the two causes?
checks.explanation: Two silent failures. The one-shot recognition call is designed for a single short utterance: it stops at the first silence and returns, so everything after the caller's opening sentence is simply never transcribed — long audio needs continuous recognition with callbacks or the asynchronous batch interface. And the emotional-style element lives in a vendor-specific namespace: if that namespace is not declared on the root element, the element is meaningless and the voice comes out neutral, which is exactly the 'why is my voice still neutral' bug. Note also that styles are per-voice, so even a correctly declared style may not be supported by the voice you chose.
options: The single-utterance recognition call stops at the first silence and returns one result — long audio needs continuous recognition with event callbacks, or the asynchronous batch interface over stored files. And the emotional-style element belongs to a vendor-specific namespace that must be declared on the root element; without that declaration the element does nothing and the voice stays neutral, with no error to notice

The transcripts are truncated because the audio exceeded the per-request size limit, which requires splitting the file; the flat delivery means the prosody rate was set to zero, which overrides the style
Both come from the wrong region: a mismatched region silently degrades to a basic model that neither continues past one utterance nor supports styles
The truncation means the audio was not sixteen-bit mono, so only the first channel was read; the flat delivery means the chosen voice is a standard rather than neural voice

checks.prompt: Model the pricing and the markup document — nothing is sent. Define `TTS_RATES` mapping `"Neural"` to 15.0 per million characters with 500000 free, `"HD"` to 30.0 with none free and `"Custom"` to 24.0 with none free; `STT_RATES` mapping `"RealTime"` and `"Batch"` to 1.0 per audio hour with 5 free hours and `"Custom"` to 1.40 with none; and the two namespace constants `SYNTHESIS_NS = "http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis"` and `MSTTS_NS = "https://www.w3.org/2001/mstts"`. Write `tts_cost(chars, tier)` and `stt_cost(hours, tier)`, each charging only the amount beyond the free allowance and raising `ValueError` for an unknown tier. Write `build_ssml(text, voice, style=None, role=None, rate=None, pitch=None, voice_styles=None)` returning the document as a string. Raise `ValueError` unless the voice name ends in `"Neural"` and has at least three hyphen-separated parts, and — when a style is given — unless `voice_styles` lists it for that voice. Escape the text and quote every attribute value. Wrap the text in a `prosody` element carrying whichever of `rate` and `pitch` were given, if either was; then wrap THAT in an `mstts:express-as` element carrying whichever of `style` and `role` were given, if either was. The root is `<speak version='1.0' …>` carrying `xmlns` set to the synthesis namespace, `xmlns:mstts` set to the vendor namespace ONLY when a style or role is present, and `xml:lang` set to the first two hyphen-separated parts of the voice name; inside it sits a `voice` element carrying the voice name and the body. Write `billable_characters(document)` returning its length. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Three things are being pinned. First, the two features are metered on different units — characters for synthesis, hours of audio for recognition — each with its own free allowance, so a voicebot's bill is two separate estimates rather than one. Second, the namespace declaration is conditional and load-bearing: the plain document does not declare the vendor namespace, and the styled one must, because without it the expressive element is not merely ignored — it is meaningless, and the voice comes out neutral with nothing to notice. Refusing a style the voice does not support catches the same class of silent nothing one step earlier. Third, the text is markup: an unescaped ampersand or angle bracket produces a document that cannot be parsed at all, so escaping is not tidiness. And the closing assertions make the commercial point — a twelve-character sentence becomes a document several times longer, and every one of those characters is billed.
checks.test:
from xml.dom import minidom

# The two features are metered on different units entirely -- characters for
# synthesis, audio hours for recognition -- so they have to be estimated separately.
assert tts_cost(1_000_000, "Neural") == 7.5
assert tts_cost(500_000, "Neural") == 0.0
assert tts_cost(1_000_000, "HD") == 30.0
assert tts_cost(1_000_000, "Custom") == 24.0
assert stt_cost(100, "RealTime") == 95.0
assert stt_cost(5, "Batch") == 0.0
assert stt_cost(100, "Custom") == 140.0
assert stt_cost(0, "RealTime") == 0.0
for bad in (lambda: tts_cost(10, "Basic"), lambda: stt_cost(10, "Streaming")):
    try:
        bad()
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError("an unknown tier must be refused")

# The plain document declares only the standard namespace.
plain = build_ssml("Hello there.", "en-US-JennyNeural")
document = minidom.parseString(plain)
speak = document.documentElement
assert speak.tagName == "speak"
assert speak.getAttribute("xmlns") == "http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis"
assert speak.getAttribute("xml:lang") == "en-US"
assert speak.getAttribute("xmlns:mstts") == ""
assert speak.getElementsByTagName("voice")[0].getAttribute("name") == "en-US-JennyNeural"
assert speak.getElementsByTagName("prosody") == []
assert "Hello there." in plain

# The moment an emotional style is used, the vendor namespace MUST be declared --
# without it the element is meaningless and the voice stays neutral, silently.
STYLES = {"en-US-JennyNeural": ("cheerful", "sad", "customerservice"),
          "en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural": ("newscast",)}
styled = build_ssml("Great news.", "en-US-JennyNeural", style="cheerful",
                    voice_styles=STYLES)
document = minidom.parseString(styled)
speak = document.documentElement
assert speak.getAttribute("xmlns:mstts") == "https://www.w3.org/2001/mstts", styled
expressive = document.getElementsByTagName("mstts:express-as")
assert len(expressive) == 1 and expressive[0].getAttribute("style") == "cheerful"
assert "xmlns:mstts" not in plain, "the namespace is only declared when it is used"

# Styles are a property of the VOICE, so asking a voice for one it does not have is
# refused here rather than being quietly ignored by the service.
try:
    build_ssml("Great news.", "en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural", style="cheerful",
               voice_styles=STYLES)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unsupported style must be refused")
build_ssml("Great news.", "en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural", style="newscast",
           voice_styles=STYLES)

# Prosody wraps the text only when something was asked for.
shaped = build_ssml("Slow down.", "en-US-JennyNeural", rate="-10%", pitch="+2st")
prosody = minidom.parseString(shaped).getElementsByTagName("prosody")[0]
assert prosody.getAttribute("rate") == "-10%" and prosody.getAttribute("pitch") == "+2st"
assert minidom.parseString(
    build_ssml("x", "en-US-JennyNeural", rate="+5%")).getElementsByTagName(
        "prosody")[0].getAttribute("pitch") == ""

# Style and prosody nest, with the expressive element outside.
both = build_ssml("Hi.", "en-US-JennyNeural", style="sad", rate="-5%",
                  voice_styles=STYLES)
outer = minidom.parseString(both).getElementsByTagName("mstts:express-as")[0]
assert outer.getElementsByTagName("prosody"), both

# Text is markup, so it has to be escaped -- otherwise a stray character produces a
# document the service cannot parse at all.
risky = build_ssml("Tom & Jerry <3 5 > 4", "en-US-JennyNeural")
minidom.parseString(risky)
assert "&" in risky and "<" in risky, risky
assert minidom.parseString(risky).getElementsByTagName("voice")[0] \
    .firstChild.data == "Tom & Jerry <3 5 > 4"

# The locale on the document is taken from the voice, so the two cannot disagree.
assert minidom.parseString(build_ssml("x", "de-DE-KatjaNeural")) \
    .documentElement.getAttribute("xml:lang") == "de-DE"
for bad in ("JennyNeural", "en-US-Jenny", "en-US-JennyNeural-v2"):
    try:
        build_ssml("x", bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad!r} must be refused")

# Every character of the document is billed, so the markup itself has a price --
# a short sentence can cost several times its own length once wrapped.
assert billable_characters(plain) == len(plain)
assert billable_characters(plain) > 4 * len("Hello there.")
assert billable_characters(styled) > billable_characters(
    build_ssml("Great news.", "en-US-JennyNeural"))
assert tts_cost(billable_characters(plain), "Neural") == \
    tts_cost(len(plain), "Neural")

checks.prompt: A pilot behaves oddly: calls appear to succeed but produce empty text and no exception; a load test on the free tier fails with throttling; and audio synthesised for a phone system is unusable. Which set of explanations is right?
checks.explanation: Three practical realities of this toolkit. Errors surface as a result whose reason says cancelled together with cancellation details naming the cause — authentication, quota, bad audio — rather than as an exception, so code that assumes success sees empty text and no error. The free tier is deliberately rate-limited with low concurrency and a monthly cap, so it is the wrong place to benchmark throughput. And the synthesis output format is a deliberate choice: telephony, web delivery and signal processing each want something different, and the default is unlikely to be what a phone network needs.
options: Failures do not raise — a call returns a result whose reason says it was cancelled, with details carrying the error code and message, so success must be checked rather than assumed. The free tier has low concurrency and monthly caps, so it throttles under load and real throughput must be measured on the paid tier. And the synthesis output format has to be set explicitly to match the consumer: a phone system wants a low-rate telephony format, the web wants a compressed one, and further signal processing wants uncompressed samples
Empty results mean the audio was silent, which is also why the load test failed; and the phone audio is unusable because telephony requires the recognition side rather than the synthesis side
All three are region mismatches: the region is validated lazily, so an incorrect one produces empty results, throttling and wrong-format audio together

Empty results mean the recognition language was not set and defaults to a different locale; throttling on the free tier is a transient service issue that retries resolve; and telephony audio requires a custom voice

checks.prompt: Compare this platform with the equivalent services from the other two major clouds, with the specialist naturalness leader, and with self-hosted open models. Say what each wins on and what it costs. Then advise a language-learning company that needs to score learners' pronunciation, transcribe their attempts, speak example sentences in twelve languages, and eventually offer a recognisable brand voice — and say what you would tell them about the last requirement.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all four. This platform wins on covering recognition, synthesis, translation, speaker recognition and pronunciation scoring through one toolkit and one resource, across a very large number of locales, with the cloud's identity, network-control and compliance plumbing; the costs are that it is cloud-only, that its expressive synthesis trails the specialist, and per-use billing on two separate meters. The other clouds' speech services are comparable in quality and are the right answer when you are native to those platforms, though they tend to split recognition and synthesis into separate products rather than one unified toolkit. The specialist wins decisively on naturalness and instant voice cloning but is synthesis-focused with a weaker recognition story and no enterprise plumbing of this kind. Self-hosted open models win on running offline with no per-use bill and audio never leaving the machine, at the cost of running the infrastructure and quality that trails. The recommendation must be this platform, and the reason must be the pronunciation-assessment requirement specifically: it is a first-class feature here and is not something the alternatives offer, and it arrives alongside the recognition and multilingual synthesis the same product needs — one integration rather than three. The brand-voice requirement must be handled honestly: a custom brand voice exists but is a gated programme requiring an application, a responsible-use review and studio-quality recordings, so it is a project with a lead time rather than a feature to switch on; if quick cloning from a short sample is what they actually want, that is the specialist's territory and would mean a second vendor. Noting that synthesis and recognition are billed on different units, so their volumes must be estimated separately, is a plus.
